questions.text: How do you write a simple closure that increments its argument `x` by 1?

answers.text: `closure x { x + 1 }`

questions.explanation: Closure parameters are written between vertical bars, followed by the body: `|x| x + 1`.

questions.text: What happens if `let identity = |x| x;` is first called with a `String` and then with an `i32`?

answers.text: The second call does not fit: the closure parameter and return types were already inferred from the first use
The closure automatically becomes generic and accepts both types
Both calls always return a `String`
The compiler chooses the type only at runtime

questions.explanation: Closure types may be inferred, but after inference they are fixed for that closure. A closure is not automatically a generic function.

questions.text: How can a closure capture values from its environment? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: By immutable reference
By mutable reference
By taking ownership
Only through global variables

questions.explanation: The book relates environment capture to familiar access forms: `&T`, `&mut T`, and ownership transfer of `T`.

questions.text: Which statements about the `move` keyword before a closure are true? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: It forces the closure to take ownership of captured values
It is especially useful when sending a closure to another thread
The presence of `move` alone does not mean the body will move a value out of the closure when called
It disables ownership rules inside the closure

questions.explanation: `move` determines capture mode by transferring values into the closure. The implemented `Fn` traits still depend on what the body does with them.

questions.text: Which trait does every closure implement at minimum?

answers.text: `FnOnce`
`Iterator`
`Drop`
`Deref`

questions.explanation: Every closure implements `FnOnce` because every closure can be viewed as callable at least once.

questions.text: Which statements about `Fn`, `FnMut`, and `FnOnce` are true? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: `FnOnce` allows closures that may move a captured value out of themselves
`FnMut` allows mutation of captured state
`Fn` fits closures that neither mutate nor move captured state
`Fn` means the closure must be called exactly once

questions.explanation: The three traits describe repeatability and how the closure treats captured state. `Fn` is the most restrictive about mutation, not a one-call requirement.

questions.text: What happens immediately after `let iter = v.iter();` if the iterator is never used further?

answers.text: No elements are processed yet: iterators are lazy
The vector is immediately dropped
All elements are automatically cloned
`iter()` immediately calls `collect()`

questions.explanation: Creating an iterator alone does not process elements; work happens when the iterator is consumed.

questions.text: Which statements about `Iterator::next` are true? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: It returns `Some(item)` while elements remain
It returns `None` when the elements are exhausted
Calling it changes iterator state, so it takes `&mut self`
It always returns `&T` regardless of iterator type

questions.explanation: The core method is `next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item>`; the concrete item type depends on the iterator.

questions.text: How do `iter()`, `iter_mut()`, and `into_iter()` differ? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: `iter()` iterates over borrowed `&T` values
`iter_mut()` yields mutable `&mut T` values
`into_iter()` gives the collection to the iterator and yields owned elements
All three always leave the original collection fully usable without restrictions

questions.explanation: The iterator-construction method determines the ownership relationship: shared borrow, mutable borrow, or ownership transfer.

questions.text: What does `sum()` do when called on an iterator?

answers.text: It consumes the iterator and computes the final sum
It returns a new lazy iterator without computing
It changes every source element to the sum
It always returns `Option`

questions.explanation: `sum` is a consuming operation that walks the sequence and produces a final result.

questions.text: Why does `v.iter().map(|x| x + 1);` by itself not transform all elements?

answers.text: `map` creates a new lazy iterator that must be consumed
`map` works only with `String`
The closure must be `FnOnce`
`iter()` is always empty

questions.explanation: `map` is an iterator adapter: it describes a transformation, and evaluation happens when the new iterator is consumed.

questions.text: Which statements about `filter` are true? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: It accepts a closure returning `bool`
It keeps elements for which the closure returns `true`
It can use variables captured from the environment
It always consumes the original collection regardless of how the iterator was created

questions.explanation: `filter` creates a new iterator and uses a predicate closure. Ownership depends on whether the chain starts with `iter`, `iter_mut`, or `into_iter`.

questions.text: Which statements correctly classify the listed iterator operations? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: `map` creates a new iterator
`filter` creates a new iterator
`collect` consumes an iterator
`sum` consumes an iterator
`map` immediately consumes the entire iterator and returns a ready `Vec`

questions.explanation: `map` and `filter` are lazy adapters, while `collect` and `sum` consume the iterator to produce a result.

questions.text: Which statements about the performance of Rust iterators are true? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Iterator style can compile to efficient low-level code
Iterators are presented as an example of zero-cost abstractions
A high-level iterator chain does not imply mandatory extra runtime overhead for the abstraction
Every `map` is always exactly twice as slow as a manual loop

questions.explanation: The chapter relates iterator style to zero-cost abstractions: high-level expression does not require mandatory extra runtime cost.

questions.text: Why can `unwrap_or_else(|| expensive_fallback())` be preferable to `unwrap_or(expensive_fallback())` for an `Option<T>`?

answers.text: The fallback closure is evaluated only when the `Option` is `None`
`unwrap_or_else` always evaluates the fallback before inspecting the `Option`
`unwrap_or_else` converts `Option<T>` into `Result<T, E>`
`unwrap_or_else` makes the fallback asynchronous

questions.explanation: `unwrap_or_else` accepts a closure and invokes it lazily only for `None`; the argument to `unwrap_or` is evaluated eagerly.

questions.text: How can Rust closure syntax differ from ordinary function syntax? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Parameters are written between `| |`
Parameter and result types can often be omitted
Braces can be omitted for a one-expression body
A closure must have a name after `fn`

questions.explanation: The book demonstrates concise closure syntax and compiler type inference.

questions.text: What happens if a closure immutably borrows `list` and, after the closure's last use, the code prints `list` again?

answers.text: This is allowed: the closure's borrow is no longer used
It is forbidden until the end of the function
`list` is automatically moved into the closure
`move` must be added

questions.explanation: The example shows that a borrow created by capture can end after the closure's last use.

questions.text: Which statements are true when a closure captures `list` through a mutable reference? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: The closure can modify `list`
Other access to `list` is restricted by borrowing rules while the borrow is active
The borrow can end after the closure's last use
`move` is required for every mutating closure

questions.explanation: Environment capture follows ordinary `&mut` rules; `move` controls ownership rather than whether mutation occurs.

questions.text: Why might the compiler require `move` for a closure passed to a new thread?

answers.text: The thread may outlive the current function, so a reference to a local value could become invalid
`move` makes the thread synchronous
Closures cannot be called without `move`
`move` automatically clones all values

questions.explanation: `move` transfers the environment into the closure, which is useful when the closure may execute after the current scope ends.

questions.text: How does the closure body affect which `Fn` traits it implements? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Moving a captured value out limits the closure to `FnOnce`
Mutating a captured value requires at least `FnMut`
Only reading the environment is compatible with `Fn`
The `move` keyword by itself always means only `FnOnce`, regardless of the body

questions.explanation: The implemented traits are determined by what the body does with captured values; `move` only changes capture mode.

questions.text: Why is an iterator variable declared `mut` when calling `next()` explicitly?

answers.text: `next()` changes iterator state by advancing it
Because the elements themselves must be mutable
To make the vector mutable
Only because of `assert_eq!`

questions.explanation: `Iterator::next` takes `&mut self` because it tracks and advances its position.

questions.text: What do successive `next()` calls return for `vec![1,2,3].iter()`? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: First `Some(&1)`
Then `Some(&2)` and `Some(&3)`
After exhaustion, `None`
After `None`, the iterator automatically starts over

questions.explanation: The example yields successive `Some` values and then `None` after exhaustion.

questions.text: What happens to an iterator after calling the consuming method `sum()`?

answers.text: The method takes ownership of the iterator, so it cannot be used again
It automatically rewinds to the beginning
`sum` only immutably borrows the iterator
The iterator becomes a `Vec`

questions.explanation: Consuming methods take `self` and produce a final value.

questions.text: Which statements about lazy iterator adapters are true? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: `map` by itself does not process all elements
An adapter chain must eventually be consumed
`collect` can trigger computation of the chain
Lazy adapters never execute even when consumed

questions.explanation: `map` creates a lazy iterator; the work happens once the chain is consumed.

questions.text: For `Iterator::filter`, if the iterator's item type is `T`, what does the predicate closure receive?

answers.text: A reference `&T` to each item being considered
Ownership of the entire source `Vec<T>` on every call
Only the item index without the value
A `Result<T, E>` regardless of the iterator type
A mutable reference `&mut T` in every case

questions.explanation: `filter` passes the predicate a reference to the item (`&Self::Item`) so checking the predicate does not itself consume the item; matching items remain the items produced by the iterator pipeline.

questions.text: How is a missing next argument represented in the iterator-based version? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: `next()` returns `Option<String>`
`None` means there is no argument
A `match` can return a clear `Err`
Indexing `args[1]` remains mandatory

questions.explanation: The iterator version handles the `Option` returned by `next()` instead of indexing.

questions.text: Which advantages can an iterator-based implementation of `search` provide? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: The code focuses on the high-level filtering goal
There is no need to manually create and fill a result vector
Loop boilerplate is hidden behind adapters
Iterators are guaranteed to be faster in every task

questions.explanation: The book emphasizes readability and high-level intent, not unconditional speed superiority.

questions.text: What does zero-cost abstraction mean for iterators? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: The abstraction should not impose mandatory runtime overhead
The compiler can produce code comparable to a manual low-level implementation
You do not pay at runtime for an unused capability
The machine code must always be shorter

questions.explanation: Iterators are presented as an abstraction without mandatory additional execution cost.

questions.text: What is the `Item` type of `v.iter()` for `Vec<i32>`?

answers.text: A reference to an element, such as `&i32`
Always an owned `i32`
The `Vec<i32>` itself
`Option<Vec<i32>>`

questions.explanation: `iter()` iterates over immutable references.

questions.text: Which iterator-construction method matches each ownership requirement? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Read only — `iter()`
Mutate through references — `iter_mut()`
Take ownership of elements — `into_iter()`
`Item` must be identical in all cases

questions.explanation: The material maps the three methods to different forms of access to elements.

questions.text: Which properties of Rust closures and iterators are true? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: They are inspired by functional languages
They express high-level ideas
They can preserve low-level performance
They require a runtime interpreter

questions.explanation: The summary connects closures and iterators with expressiveness and the zero-cost approach.
